The Desert long-eared bat Otonycteris hemprichii exhibits a relatively low reproductive output for a vespertilionid of its size, based on extrapolations from closely related congeners. Females are estimated to produce a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and raise only one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], a pattern that aligns with the slow life-history strategy observed in many arid-zone bats. This annual reproductive rate is thought to be constrained by the unpredictable availability of insect prey across the deserts of North Africa and the Middle East. Neonates are born altricial, weighing approximately 5.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.5 grams], which represents a substantial investment relative to the ultimate adult female mass. This birth mass is roughly one-fifth of the mother's adult size, a ratio common among bats that produce a single, well-provisioned offspring. The species is not known to exhibit delayed implantation or embryonic diapause, and the timing of parturition is closely tied to the seasonal peak in arthropod abundance during the spring months.

Under the thermal conditions typical of a normothermic, resting bat at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], the gestation period of the Desert long-eared bat is estimated at 65 days [tg = 65 days], a duration consistent with that reported for the closely related long-eared bat Plecotus auritus. This relatively extended gestation is characteristic of temperate and subtropical vespertilionids that produce a single pup and invest heavily in neonatal development prior to birth. Following parturition, the dependent neonate enters a suckling stage that lasts for several weeks. This weaning age reflects the considerable effort required to bring the juvenile to a body size and flight capability sufficient for independent foraging.

The age at first reproduction is therefore likely synchronized with the attainment of full adult body size and social integration into the colony. The delay between weaning and puberty is a notable feature of this species' life-history, potentially linked to the high costs of foraging in an arid landscape where insect prey is patchily distributed and seasonal.

Adult females of the Desert long-eared bat achieve an ultimate body mass of 25.4 grams [Wwi = 25.4 grams], a size that positions them among the larger insectivorous bats of the Palearctic region. This substantial body mass is associated with a metabolic rate measured under standard conditions. At a body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate recorded for this species is 16.30 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 16.30 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the energetic demands of maintaining homeostasis and supporting the foraging activity required to subsist on a diet of beetles, scorpions, and other large arthropods. This relatively elevated metabolic rate for a desert insectivore underscores the species' reliance on a high-protein diet to meet its daily energetic requirements, especially during the breeding season when females must support both their own maintenance and the growth of a single pup.

The maximum lifespan of Otonycteris hemprichii in the wild, inferred from long-term studies of the analogous species Plecotus auritus, is estimated to be approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] when measured at a typical resting temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This extreme longevity, rare among small mammals, is a hallmark of the slow life-history syndrome seen in many chiropterans, characterized by low annual fecundity, delayed sexual maturity, and extended somatic maintenance. The near absence of predation pressure in arid environments and the ability to enter daily torpor during periods of food scarcity are likely physiological mechanisms that contribute to this extended lifespan, allowing individuals to survive harsh conditions that would prove lethal to most terrestrial mammals of comparable size.
